title: Salutation to the Merciful
hook: namastvam kripaale: salutation to the Merciful One (Jaap, bhujang prayat)

segments.voice: Yesterday, akaal, the Timeless and Deathless, and your line, beyond time. Did a glance at the clock become a slow breath? Today, the very next line of the glide. Day three hundred thirty-eight.

A parking ticket, a library fine, a late assignment. You walk up ready to argue, already tired, and the person behind the counter looks at you, looks at the clock, and says: don't worry about it this time. That's it. No speech. Just a small door opening where you expected a wall. Moments like that tend to stay. Mercy has a way of doing that. And in Jaap Sahib, right after the bow to the One beyond time, comes a bow to exactly this. Today: salutation to the Merciful.
screen: `A FINE, A TICKET, A LATE ASSIGNMENT.` → `DON'T WORRY ABOUT IT THIS TIME.` → `A DOOR WHERE YOU EXPECTED A WALL.`

segments.voice: The line is namastvam kripaale. A bow to you, the Merciful. Kripaal comes from kirpa, or kripa: grace, kindness, mercy, favor you didn't earn. Kripaal is the One who is full of it. Now notice the order. The first line bowed to akaal, the Timeless, the One the clock can't touch. That could sound cold, a God too big and too far away to care about a parking ticket. So the very next line answers it. Timeless, yes. And merciful. In Jaap's order, the One beyond time is also the One who shows mercy. In Sikh teaching those two ideas belong together. Guru Nanak's hymns speak of nadar, the glance of grace, the kind look that lifts a person when their own effort has run out. Japji, which you walked through last year, says liberation comes through that grace. And the word kirpa is everywhere in Punjabi life, not just in prayer books. Ask a Sikh grandmother how the family is doing, and you may well hear: Waheguru di kirpa naal, theek haan. By Waheguru's grace, we're fine. A new job, a healthy baby, a safe journey, all described as kirpa. It's a way of saying: this wasn't only my doing. And it has a practical edge. Some Sikhs hear a question tucked inside the bow: if the One I salute every morning is merciful, where could I open a small door instead of a wall today? Jaap doesn't say that in so many words. It just puts mercy second in the glide, right after eternity.
screen: `KIRPA: GRACE, KINDNESS, MERCY.` · `TIMELESS, AND THEN MERCIFUL.` · `NADAR: THE GLANCE OF GRACE.` · `WAHEGURU DI KIRPA NAAL: BY GRACE.` · then, large: `SALUTE MERCY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one act of mercy for today. Think of someone who owes you something: an apology, an answer, a favor, a return of something borrowed. Or someone who's been a little careless with you lately. Picture their face. Breathe. And decide, quietly, to let one small thing go, the way the person at the counter did. Not everything. Just one. If you pray, you can say namastvam kripaale under your breath. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
Kripaal. Merciful, full of kirpa, grace — namastvam kripaale, the second bow of Jaap's glide, right after the bow to the Timeless.
Your line: salute mercy. Today, show mercy once: let one small debt, mistake or delay go, and say nothing about it. Day three hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of good things in daily life as kirpa, grace, often saying Waheguru di kirpa naal, by Waheguru's grace, and recite namastvam kripaale each morning in Jaap Sahib.

akaal comes first, then kripaal, right after it.

fork.setup: Jaap has just bowed to the Timeless, the One the clock can't touch. a listener worries: is this God too far away to care? what does the next line say?
fork.reveal: namastvam kripaale: Jaap pairs them, timeless and merciful, one line after the other.

original.note: Gurmukhi: kripaal, merciful, the One full of kirpa, grace.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Merciful is just a gentle title.
what it means: placed right after the Timeless, it pairs the One beyond time with grace people did not earn.
what a scholar hears: kripaal derives from Sanskrit kripa, compassion; Gurbani pairs it with nadar, the gracious glance, as the source of liberation.

sources.ref: Jaap Sahib, stanza 2 (bhujang prayat): namastvam kripaale
Japji, nadar (grace) as the source of liberation (e.g., pauri 4)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): removed 'most of us remember' from the hook; the narrator no longer states 'the infinite One leans toward you' as fact (teach, fork, trapdoor now attribute it to Jaap's order); the 'what about you?' turn now describes a question some Sikhs hear instead of putting it to the listener
Kripaal from kirpa/kripa: confirm the gloss.
Japji's 'karmi aavai kaprra nadri mokh duaar' (pauri 4) is the intended reference for grace and liberation; paraphrased, not quoted. Confirm.
'Waheguru di kirpa naal, theek haan' as an everyday Punjabi phrase: confirm wording.
Avoided the popular kirpan = kirpa + aan derivation, which is debated.
